content: Tongue-tie, also known as ankyloglossia, is a condition where the lingual frenulum is attached near the tip of the tongue and may be short, tight, and thick. This condition is observed in approximately 4% to 11% of newborns. Tongue-tie has been identified as a potential cause of poor breastfeeding and maternal nipple pain. Frenotomy, a procedure commonly performed to address this issue, involves cutting the frenulum to release the restriction in tongue movement. This may improve breastfeeding effectiveness and reduce maternal nipple pain. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether frenotomy is a safe and effective intervention for improving oral feeding in infants under three months of age with tongue-tie and feeding difficulties. Additionally, subgroup analyses were conducted to assess the following factors: the severity of tongue-tie (measured using tools like the Hazelbaker Assessment Tool for Lingual Frenulum Function), gestational age at birth (preterm versus term infants), feeding method (breastfeeding versus bottle feeding), age at the time of frenotomy (≤10 days versus >10 days to three months), and the severity of feeding difficulties (e.g., infants with weight gain issues versus those thriving despite feeding challenges). The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, up to January 2017. They also reviewed previous studies, consulted expert informants, and searched clinical trial registries for ongoing or recently completed trials. No language restrictions were applied. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized, quasi-randomized, or cluster-randomized controlled trials comparing frenotomy to no frenotomy or a sham procedure in newborns. Data were extracted from the included trials to assess clinical outcomes such as infant feeding, maternal nipple pain, breastfeeding duration, cessation of breastfeeding, infant pain, excessive bleeding, infection, ulceration, tongue or submandibular duct damage, and recurrence of tongue-tie. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Five randomized trials involving a total of 302 participants met the inclusion criteria. Three studies objectively measured infant breastfeeding using standardized tools. A pooled analysis of two studies (n = 155) showed no significant change in feeding scores on a 10-point scale after frenotomy (mean difference [MD] -0.1, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.6 to 0.5). However, a third study (n = 58) demonstrated an improvement in feeding scores on a 12-point scale (MD 3.5, 95% CI 3.1 to 4.0). Four studies assessed maternal nipple pain objectively. A pooled analysis of three studies (n = 212) using a 10-point pain scale showed a reduction in maternal pain scores following frenotomy (MD -0.7, 95% CI -1.4 to -0.1). Another study (n = 58) reported a reduction in pain scores on a 50-point scale (MD -8.6, 95% CI -9.4 to -7.8). None of the studies reported adverse effects associated with frenotomy. However, the studies had significant methodological limitations. Sample sizes were small, and only two studies blinded both mothers and assessors. One study did not attempt blinding at all. Additionally, all studies offered frenotomy to control groups, and most control participants eventually underwent the procedure, indicating a lack of equipoise. None of the studies provided data on whether frenotomy resulted in long-term breastfeeding success. In conclusion, frenotomy was found to reduce maternal nipple pain in the short term. However, there was no consistent evidence of improvement in infant breastfeeding. No serious complications were reported, but the small sample sizes and methodological flaws limit the reliability of these findings. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to determine the long-term effects and overall efficacy of frenotomy.
